paragraphs: I flatter myself that my last number showed clearly that, under the proposed Constitution, the particular States would have COEQUAL authority with the Union in matters of revenue, except for duties on imports. This leaves the States far the greater part of the community's resources, so there can be no pretext for claiming that they would lack means as abundant as could be wished to supply their own wants, free of all outside control. That the field is wide enough will appear more fully when we come to the small share of the public expenses that the State governments will have to provide for.

To argue from abstract principles that this coordinate authority cannot exist is to set supposition and theory against fact and reality. Such reasoning may be proper for showing that a thing OUGHT NOT TO EXIST. It must be wholly rejected when it is used to prove that a thing does not exist, in the face of the fact itself. It is well known that in the Roman republic the legislative authority, in the last resort, rested for ages in two different political bodies. They were not branches of one legislature but distinct and independent legislatures, and in each an opposing interest prevailed: the patrician in one, the plebeian in the other. Many arguments might have been offered to prove that two such seemingly contradictory authorities, each able to ANNUL or REPEAL the acts of the other, were unfit to coexist. But anyone at Rome who tried to disprove their existence would have been thought frantic. It will be readily understood that I am referring to the COMITIA CENTURIATA and the COMITIA TRIBUTA. In the former, where the people voted by centuries, the arrangement gave the patrician interest the advantage. In the latter, where numbers prevailed, the plebeian interest was wholly predominant. And yet these two legislatures existed side by side for ages, and the Roman republic rose to the utmost height of human greatness.

In the case now before us there is no such contradiction as appears in the example I cited, because neither side has power to annul the acts of the other. In practice, too, there is little reason to fear any problem. In a short time the wants of the States will naturally shrink WITHIN A VERY NARROW COMPASS, and in the meantime the United States will in all probability find it convenient to stay entirely away from those objects to which the particular States would be inclined to turn.

To judge the true merits of this question more precisely, it will be well to look at the proportion between the objects that will require a federal provision of revenue and those that will require a State provision. We shall find that the former are altogether unlimited and the latter are held within very moderate bounds. In pursuing this inquiry we must keep in mind that we are not to look only at the present period but forward to a remote future. Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed on a calculation of present necessities alone, but on a combination of these with the probable necessities of ages, following the natural and tried course of human affairs. Nothing, therefore, can be more fallacious than to infer, from an estimate of its immediate necessities, how much power ought to be lodged in the national government. There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they arise; and since these are illimitable by nature, it is impossible to limit that capacity safely. It is true, perhaps, that one could compute, accurately enough for the purpose, how much revenue is needed to discharge the Union's existing engagements and to maintain the peacetime establishments that would suffice for some time to come. But would it be wise, or would it not rather be the extreme of folly, to stop at this point? That would leave the government entrusted with the national defense wholly incapable of protecting the community against future breaches of the public peace, whether by foreign war or domestic convulsions. If, on the contrary, we ought to go past this point, where can we stop short of an indefinite power to provide for emergencies as they arise? It is easy to assert, in general terms, that a rational judgment can be formed of a proper provision against probable dangers. But we may safely challenge those who make this assertion to produce their data, and may affirm that those data would prove as vague and uncertain as any that could be offered to establish how long the world will probably last. Observations confined to the mere prospect of internal attacks deserve no weight, though even these admit of no satisfactory calculation. And if we mean to be a commercial people, our policy must include being able one day to defend that commerce. Supporting a navy and naval wars would involve contingencies that must defeat all the efforts of political arithmetic.

Suppose we admit that we ought to try the novel and absurd experiment in politics of tying the government's hands against offensive war founded on reasons of state. Certainly we ought not to disable it from guarding the community against the ambition or enmity of other nations. A cloud has hung over the European world for some time. If it should break into a storm, who can assure us that some of its fury would not be spent on us as it moves? No reasonable man would hastily declare that we are entirely out of its reach. Or suppose the combustible materials that now seem to be gathering should disperse before coming to maturity, or a flame should be kindled that does not reach us. What security have we that our tranquillity will long remain undisturbed from some other cause or quarter? Let us remember that peace or war will not always be left to our choice. However moderate or unambitious we may be, we cannot count on the moderation of others or hope to extinguish their ambition. At the end of the last war, who could have imagined that France and Britain, wearied and exhausted as both were, would so soon look on each other with such hostility? If we judge by the history of mankind, we shall have to conclude that the fiery and destructive passions of war rule the human breast far more powerfully than the mild and beneficent feelings of peace. To model our political systems on speculations of lasting tranquillity is to calculate on the weaker springs of the human character.

What are the chief sources of expense in every government? What has caused the enormous accumulation of debts that weighs on several of the European nations? The answer is plain: wars and rebellions, and the upkeep of the institutions necessary to guard the body politic against these two most deadly diseases of society. The expenses of institutions that concern the mere domestic police of a state, the support of its legislative, executive and judicial departments with their various appendages, and the encouragement of agriculture and manufactures (which will cover almost all the objects of state expenditure) are insignificant beside those that concern the national defense.

In the kingdom of Great Britain, which must pay for all the ostentatious apparatus of monarchy, not more than a fifteenth part of the nation's annual income goes to the class of expenses I last mentioned. The other fourteen fifteenths are swallowed up by interest on the debts contracted to carry on the wars that country has fought, and by the upkeep of fleets and armies. One may observe, on the one hand, that the expenses of pursuing the ambitious enterprises and vainglorious projects of a monarchy are not a proper standard for judging what a republic might need. On the other hand, one ought to remark that there should be an equally great gap between the profusion and extravagance of a wealthy kingdom in its domestic administration and the frugality and economy that become, in this respect, the modest simplicity of republican government. If we balance a proper deduction on one side against the one that is supposed to be made on the other, the proportion may still be considered to hold.

But consider the large debt we ourselves ran up in a single war, and calculate on no more than a common share of the events that disturb the peace of nations. We shall see at once, without any elaborate illustration, that there must always be an immense disproportion between federal and State expenditures. It is true that several of the States, separately, are burdened with considerable debts, an outgrowth of the recent war. But this cannot happen again if the proposed system is adopted. When those debts are paid off, the only call for revenue of any consequence that the State governments will still have is the mere support of their respective civil lists. Adding all contingencies to this, the total in every State ought to come in considerably under two hundred thousand pounds.

In framing a government for posterity as well as for ourselves, we ought, in those provisions meant to be permanent, to calculate on permanent rather than temporary causes of expense. If this principle is just, our attention would be directed to providing the State governments with an annual sum of about two hundred thousand pounds, while the necessities of the Union could admit of no limits, even in imagination. Seen in this way, by what logic can it be maintained that the local governments ought to command, in perpetuity, an EXCLUSIVE source of revenue for any sum beyond two hundred thousand pounds? To extend their power further, in EXCLUSION of the authority of the Union, would be to take the resources of the community out of the hands that needed them for the public welfare and put them into other hands that could have no just or proper occasion for them.

Suppose, then, that the Convention had been inclined to divide the objects of revenue between the Union and its members in PROPORTION to their comparative necessities. What particular fund could have been picked out for the States that would not have been either too much or too little: too little for their present wants, too much for their future wants? Take the dividing line between external and internal taxes. By rough computation, this would leave the States command of two thirds of the community's resources to pay from a tenth to a twentieth part of its expenses, and would leave the Union one third of the resources to pay from nine tenths to nineteen twentieths of its expenses. If we abandon this boundary and are content to leave the States an exclusive power of taxing houses and lands, there would still be a great disproportion between the MEANS and the END: possession of one third of the community's resources to supply, at most, one tenth of its wants. Suppose some fund could have been picked out and set aside that was equal to the object and no greater. It would still have been inadequate to discharge the existing debts of the particular States, and would have left them dependent on the Union for a provision for this purpose.

The preceding train of observations will justify the position laid down elsewhere, that "A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union." Any separation of the objects of revenue that could have been devised would have sacrificed the great INTERESTS of the Union to the POWER of the individual States. The Convention thought the concurrent jurisdiction preferable to that subordination. It evidently has at least the merit of reconciling an indefinite constitutional power of taxation in the federal government with an adequate and independent power in the States to provide for their own necessities. A few other lights remain in which this important subject of taxation will claim further consideration.
